text:
You give your agents a shell, and you see what they do with it. 

 
 An MCP server for SSH. Let Claude Code , Claude Desktop and OpenAI Codex (or any MCP client) 
 work on your real servers — run commands, move files, query databases, take backups, check health — 
 and watch over their shoulder while they do it.
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 Twenty seconds, unedited — watch full size . Real SSH, real SFTP, three throwaway hosts on the loopback. 
 

---

 The problem, in one line

An MCP SSH server is the most dangerous tool you can hand an agent: a shell on machines that matter. Today, when your agent runs something on production, you find out afterwards — if you find out at all.

 This one lets you watch, and lets you say no. It is also, on the boring days, simply a very good way to let an assistant do the server work you were going to do yourself.

---

 Choose your workspace

 Desktop application ( 4.4.1 ): one installation with its own runtime,
terminal, file browser and server settings. No separate Node.js or npm
installation. Download it:

 Platform File Signature 
 --- --- --- 
 macOS, Apple silicon / Intel …-arm64.dmg / …-x64.dmg Signed and notarized by Apple — opens normally 
 Windows x64 / arm64 …-setup.exe Not code-signed yet. Windows shows "Windows protected your PC" : More info → Run anyway . Check the file against the SHA-256 in release-manifest-win32.json on the release ( ssh-manager app does it for you). Signing comes in a later release. 
 Linux x64 .deb , .AppImage Unsigned, as Linux packages usually are 

 Already using npm / the CLI? npm update -g mcp-ssh-manager brings 4.4.1,
and the V4 engine runs without an interface, from your existing .env , TOML or
process variables — no automatic import, no forced wizard, no approval prompt
unless you enable one per server. The one behaviour that tightens is SSH
host-key verification ; read that section of the
upgrade and rollback guide before upgrading. To stay on 3.8
for now, pin it: npm install -g mcp-ssh-manager@3 .

 From the engine to the application in one step. With a V4 engine installed,
 ssh-manager app downloads the desktop application of the engine's own version,
checks it against the release (size and SHA-256 from the release manifest, and
on macOS Apple's signature and notarization), installs it and opens it — or just
opens it when it is already there. The browser interface of ssh-manager control 
offers the same as one button. Your agents keep using the npm engine; the
application is the window on top of it. Nothing is downloaded unless you ask.

 Without npm at all. The application carries the engine too, and your AI
tools can start that one: Options → AI tools lists Claude Code, Claude Desktop
and Codex, says which ssh-manager each one starts (npm's, the application's, or
none yet) and switches it in one click — no Node, no terminal. The same tab, in
 ssh-manager control , shows npm users which version each tool really runs.
A switch rewrites that tool's one ssh-manager entry, keeps its environment
variables, and takes effect when the tool next starts; switching back is the
same click.

 Updates. The application checks for a new version at launch and every six
hours and says so where you will see it: a mark on the sidebar, Options →
Updates (the running version, the one on offer, a Check now button, release
notes) and, once per version, a notification. Downloading is a click, and
installing is a second one ( Restart to update ) or happens when you quit. The
npm engine updates with npm, on its own schedule. A change to the interface
reaches npm users with the next npm release and application users with the next
application release.

 From source: 

 

The MCP engine needs no build. To use the interface ( ssh-manager control ) from a
checkout, build it once: npm run build:ui (the published package and the desktop
app already carry it).

 Scopes — --scope project writes an .mcp.json your team can commit; --scope user enables it everywhere for you.

 Prerequisites — Node 18+, on Linux, macOS or Windows. rsync for ssh sync , sshpass only if you sync with password auth ( brew install hudochenkov/sshpass/sshpass , or apt-get install sshpass ).

 

---

 Then just ask

No syntax to learn. Your assistant already knows how to use the 37 tools; you talk to it in your own words.

 You say What happens 
 --- --- 
 "Why is production slow right now?" CPU, memory, disk, load average and the top processes, in one round trip 
 "Back up the database before I deploy." A compressed, timestamped MySQL/PostgreSQL/MongoDB dump with a retention policy 
 "Tail the nginx error log on staging." Live output, streamed as it happens 
 "Push ./dist to production:/var/www and restart nginx." The files out, then the restart — with ownership, permissions and a rollback copy handled 
 "Which of my servers is running out of disk?" Every server in the group, checked in parallel 
 "Open a tunnel to the production database." Local port forward, so your GUI client just connects 
 "Run docker ps on everything tagged production." One command, the whole group, sequential or parallel 

 
 
 

 
 There is a CLI too, for when you'd rather do it yourself: ssh-manager with no arguments opens this. 
 

---

 Watch over its shoulder — the control plane

 New in 4.0.0. The application is opt-in: with no vault and no approval enabled, the engine keeps working headlessly, exactly as 3.8.x. See the migration guide for host-key verification and recovery behaviour.
